title: Humbler than the grass
hookLine: a shout from a car window, and a drum that keeps going
carry: chant the name humbler than grass
tomorrow: why does the food stop at the altar before anyone eats?

lines: A SHOUT FROM A CAR WINDOW.
cards: A car window rolls down, someone yells something rude, and the car speeds off before anyone can answer. Faces go hot. That happens to the singers on the sidewalk too.

And the drum keeps going, the cymbals keep time, and nobody in saffron shouts back. That's not an accident. It goes back to a short verse their own saint left them, about grass, a tree, and who gets the honor.

teach.b: Tradition credits Chaitanya with the Shikshashtakam, the eight teachings. Its third verse is about the state of mind the name should be chanted in. In paraphrase: think of yourself as lower than the grass in the street.
Be more tolerant than a tree. Expect no honor for yourself, and give honor to everyone else. A person like that, the verse says, can chant the name always.
Feel what those pictures do. Grass under a bare foot bends flat, and when the foot lifts, it springs back up.
A tree, the Chaitanya Charitamrita explains, doesn't complain when it's cut, and still gives shade to whoever sits under it. Devotees have a living picture of the verse: Haridasa, from yesterday.

His biographers tell that a local ruler had him flogged through twenty-two marketplaces for chanting Krishna's name. He kept chanting, and prayed that the men beating him would not be punished for it.

teach.h: NOT WORTHLESS: JUST NOT NEEDING IT.
teach.b: This isn't pretending to be worthless. Grass isn't ashamed of being grass. It just doesn't need the foot to apologize.
So chanting in public was never meant to be a show that needs applause. It's humility practiced in the open, and the shout from the car becomes part of it. A devotee can fall short, like anyone.

teach.h: PATIENT AS A TREE, UNDER WHOEVER PASSES.
teach.b: But the standard sits at the foundation of the movement: lower than the grass, patient as a tree, honor given away.

how: Devotees in Chaitanya's line recite or sing the Shikshashtakam, and take its third verse as the attitude for chanting the holy name.

o: singers whose saint asked them to chant humbler than grass
street performers who sing to collect donations for a temple
a protest group that chants to answer its critics loudly

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: expect none, give it to everyone
prayed for the men who beat him

s: chanting on the street is meant to win attention and applause
Chaitanya's verse asks the chanter to expect no honor at all.
Chaitanya's verse says to chant once others show you honor
it says to expect no honor yourself, and give honor to everyone.
in the Charitamrita, the tree doesn't complain even when it's cut
it doesn't ask for water while drying out, either.

games.q: at your weekend job, a customer snaps at you over something that wasn't your fault. what does Chaitanya's verse point to?
o: stay steady and give respect without needing it back, like the tree.
say it was all your fault, since being humble means taking the blame.
give respect once they've shown you some first; then it's earned.
games.why: expect no honor, give honor to everyone, be tolerant as a tree. humility here isn't pretending you're to blame; it's not needing the shout answered.

practice: Devotees keep this verse close when they chant. Sit tall, let your shoulders settle a little lower than usual, palms down on your thighs as if on cool grass.
Then say a name of God softly three times, Krishna, Rama, whichever is yours, giving it the honor you'd give a guest.
If you don't pray, on each out-breath loosen your grip on needing the next person to think well of you, and feel the ground hold you up anyway.

wordCard.voice: The Hare Krishnas: singers whose saint asked them to chant from a place humbler than the grass.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shikshashtakam, from shiksha, teaching, and ashtaka, a set of eight.

carryVoice: For the road, from Chaitanya's verse: chant the name humbler than grass, patient as a tree. That's the day.

sources.ref: Shikshashtakam, verse 3 (humbler than grass, more tolerant than a tree, giving honor and expecting none; such a one can chant always)
Chaitanya Charitamrita, Antya-lila 20 (the verse quoted and explained: the tree does not protest when cut, nor ask for water while drying)
Chaitanya Bhagavata, Adi-khanda 16 (Haridasa is beaten through twenty-two marketplaces for chanting the name and prays that his tormentors not be punished)
